transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-05
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Tom Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM), Marta Silva (Archipelago VP Eng), Devon Park (Archipelago SRE), Lin Wu (Archipelago Security), Elliot Chan (Archipelago Procurement)

Summary:
Quick alignment after last week's incident where a mid-day KV cache eviction wave amplified latency; focus today is on hardening the SLA language, agreeing fallback/routing contracts, and scheduling a dedicated stress bench. Action items and owners captured.

Topics: SLA language, fallback routing, KV cache evictions, canary and rollback policy, private deployment vs hosted failover, telemetry and audit logs, SOC2/KMS requirements, cost tradeoffs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Tom Ellis: All right afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick agenda — we'll recap the incident timeline, go over fallback and threshold cali — calibration that you asked for, and then talk contractual language.
[00:18] Marta Silva: Thanks Tom. Appreciate the follow up. So from our end we still have questions about why the eviction wave cascaded the way it did, and most importantly how the fallback contract ensures we don't see SLA hits during our morning peak, which is 09:00–11:00 PT.
[00:36] Priya Raman: hi Marta, quick framing: the pattern we saw was a hot-prefix churn — some longer tokens + repeated long context meant the KV cache grew beyond the eviction threshold and then the autoscaler couldn't replenish as fast because of the prewarming gap. It's, uh, basically a warmup/eviction interplay.
[00:58] Devon Park: yeah that's the bit — during the surge could you have routed to a quantized model variant to keep latency low, or would that have blown quality? we were worried about hallucinations.
[01:20] Priya Raman: good callout. We have model variants that are quantized — in our experience they add slight variance in output, but for routing policy we can define a quality budget: e.g. up to X% of requests can route to a faster quantized fallback during sustained priority traffic. That tradeoff should be explicit in the SLA appendix.
[01:44] Lin Wu: From security side we need to confirm if fallback routing still leaves any data in customer-managed VPC logs or whether Redwood sees any payloads in fallback mode. Need that documented for our compliance team.
[02:06] Tom Ellis: absolutely, Lin. We can guarantee that for Private deployments the payload never leaves the VPC unless you opt-in; for hosted fallback we can use encrypted transit plus tokenized redaction. We'll add an explicit KMS/HSM flow diagram to the appendix.
[02:24] Elliot Chan: what about cost? if you auto-fallback to dedicated bursting during peak, costs spike. Procurement needs predictable anchors.
[02:40] Jordan Lee: we hear that a lot — the Optimize toolkit can set hard cost gates and autoscale cap, and we can add a contractual cap or alerting thresholds in the SOW. We'll propose a cost tether clause.
[03:05] Marta Silva: ok, the other thing — your runbook had a canary that didn't trigger because the canary window overlapped the eviction; we lost confidence that automatic rollback would happen quickly.
[03:26] Priya Raman: mm-hmm. The canary heuristic we shipped uses token-timing and P50 shift detection; in this event the P50 rose slowly but P95 spiked, so the simple canary didn't trip. We recommend a multi-metric canary: P95, error-rate, and KV miss-rate.
[03:54] Devon Park: and if that still fails, what's the manual escalation path? our oncall needs a clear playbook rather than vague guidance.
[04:10] Tom Ellis: agreed. We'll add an oncall playbook appendix with the exact sequence: automatic fallback to quantized model variant -> autoscaler burst -> route to dedicated pool (if contract allows) -> engage SE, and if none of that reduces 1-minute P90 we trigger an immediate rollback.
[04:35] Marta Silva: can we make that a 4-step contractual SLA enforcement so we can tie credits to missed steps?
[04:48] Tom Ellis: yes, we can enumerate obligations and corresponding remedies; our legal has a template for SLA credits tied to detection time and mitigation time.
[05:02] Priya Raman: quick tech detail: the KV cache eviction we saw was exacerbated by a long-running generation that kept KV pinned, and when those sessions expired the eviction queued up. We think a polite garbage collection window plus preemptive KV shard throttling would reduce the amplitude. I'll propose specific thresholds.
[05:28] Devon Park: would you be able to test that in a staging env that mirrors our distribution of sequence lengths? we can share sample payload distributions.
[05:40] Priya Raman: yes please share distributions. I'll run a stress profile with 1k qps bursts and sequential tokens distribution similar to your peak. Expect logs and metrics in a shared sheet.
[05:55] Marta Silva: timeline wise we need the proposal before our exec review on the 16th.
[06:03] Tom Ellis: good — action: I'll send updated SLA language and appendix by next Friday. Priya will deliver test artifacts by Thursday.
[06:18] [00:06:18] Interruption (muted audio)
[06:40] Lin Wu: on encryption — KMS integration: do you support our HSM-backed key provider? or do we need to use Redwood-managed KMS?
[06:56] Tom Ellis: we support both. For Private deployments you can bring your own KMS with HSM; for Hosted we provide a customer-key-wrapped envelope with integrations to common KMS providers. We'll include the HSM diagram.
[07:14] Devon Park: you mentioned telemetry. In the incident we were missing token-level tracing and lost the tail-latency correlation graph. How will the new telemetry change that?
[07:32] Jordan Lee: we'll enable token-level tracing for the pilot and retain 30 days for trial. For production we can extend retention as an add-on. We'll also expose per-route P50/P95/P99 and KV miss-rate in the console.
[07:50] Marta Silva: retention and PII gating are core concerns. We need audit logs for every fallback decision for compliance.
[08:04] Tom Ellis: yes audit logs will include decision triggers, model version IDs, and routing policy IDs. We can redact content but preserve hashes for debug.
[08:18] Elliot Chan: circling back to procurement: can you provide a cost scenario for two options — strict cap with downgraded availability vs flexible routing with cost surfacing? we need numbers.
[08:36] Priya Raman: sure; I'll generate a cost matrix: option A conservative (hosted w/ strict cap, no dedicated bursting) — lower predictable spend but higher risk of latency; option B flexible (tiered fallback, dedicated pool bursting) — higher OPEX but fewer SLA hits. I'll include token/sec cost and projected monthly for your peak load.
[08:58] Devon Park: we also need to validate your autoscaler cold-start time. in our environment cold starts take longer because of internal image pulls. Will that affect the autoscaler behavior?
[09:16] Priya Raman: if your infra has slower image pulls we recommend a warm pool or reserved prewarmed instances under Dedicated capacity. That is one reason Dedicated is often recommended for predictable peak windows.
[09:33] Marta Silva: can you elaborate on Dedicated vs Hosted failover, specifically in contract terms? we saw references in the playbook but not the SOW.
[09:48] Tom Ellis: Domain wise: Hosted — Redwood controls runtime; we provide SLA for availability and lat, and fallback options are limited to policy we manage. Dedicated — reserved GPU pools in your tenancy (or our dedicated tenancy) with guaranteed prewarm; contractual guarantees are stronger for latency and capacity. We'll draft explicit language differentiating remedies.
[10:10] Lin Wu: on the security audit angle: will rolling to quantized model variants affect model provenance for regulated outputs? We need a provenance trace.
[10:28] Priya Raman: provenance is maintained — we tag model IDs and quantization profile in every response metadata header. That will be part of the audit log.
[10:40] Marta Silva: good. let's talk about the detection thresholds — what exactly will cause automatic fallback?
[10:52] Priya Raman: propose a composite trigger: P95 > X ms for Y consecutive windows OR KV miss-rate > Z% AND error-rate > Q% for T windows. We'll put explicit numbers and make them editable so you can tune as you gather telemetry.
[11:14] Devon Park: can you give a concrete example with numbers we can test?
[11:20] Priya Raman: e.g., P95 > 800ms for 3 consecutive minutes OR KV miss-rate > 12% AND error-rate > 0.5% for two minutes. We'll parameterize that.
[11:38] Marta Silva: those numbers look close to what we'd accept. But if the fallback triggers too aggressively we risk quality. Can we make the policy tiered — first quantized model for 2 minutes, then dedicated burst if persists?
[11:56] Tom Ellis: absolutely, two-stage fallback is our recommended pattern. Stage one: degrade to quantized variant for up to 5 minutes, stage two: route to reserved dedicated pool for up to configured burst, stage three: notify and if still bad then rollback.
[12:18] [00:12:18] Jordan Lee: quick note — we'll put that as flow chart in the appendix so it's legally precise.
[12:28] Elliot Chan: timeline question — if we sign the SOW with a dedicated bursting clause, how long to provision?
[12:40] Tom Ellis: for dedicated pools typically 7–14 days depending on region and inventory; we can prioritize provisioning if you commit a reservation.
[12:52] Devon Park: can Redwood support a staggered rollout so we can test small percentage of traffic through the fallback before wider roll?
[13:06] Priya Raman: yes canary by traffic slice is supported; we'll do a gradual canary with automatic metrics gating. For your environment we'll recommend a 5% -> 20% -> 100% ramp with a hold at each stage.
[13:22] Marta Silva: sounds fine. Regarding credits, we want the SLA to tie to time-to-fallback not just time-to-detect. If mitigation takes 30 minutes after detection, that's still unacceptable.
[13:36] Tom Ellis: understood. We'll draft credits that tier by detection latency and mitigation latency. Example: if detection time > 5m then X credit; if mitigation > 15m then additional credit.
[13:52] [00:13:52] Short pause (typing)
[14:08] Devon Park: technical deep dive — Priya can you run the stress test with KV prefill and do an eviction flood, then try the two-stage fallback and measure mitigation time? we want concrete p95 delta and quality delta.
[14:26] Priya Raman: yes, test plan: 1) baseline 5m steady, 2) 60s ramp to 1k qps with long contexts, 3) force KV eviction by reducing allowed cache size, 4) observe P95 and route to quantized variant at threshold, 5) route to Dedicated if persists. We'll capture token-level traces and provide the fold.
[14:46] Marta Silva: please also include a test where image pulls are slowed to simulate our cold-start behavior.
[14:54] Priya Raman: will do. add that to the test matrix.
[15:02] Lin Wu: if Dedicated is provisioned, does Redwood still have access to logs by default? we need clear opt-in for data access.
[15:16] Tom Ellis: by default Dedicated has tenant-controlled logs; Redwood can get access only with explicit consent or legal process. We'll include an access control appendix.
[15:30] Elliot Chan: procurement will want cancellation terms for reserved capacity if usage doesn't materialize.
[15:42] Jordan Lee: we'll provide a carveout: allow for a one-time adjustment in the first billing quarter with agreed thresholds.
[15:50] Marta Silva: ok runbooks and the SLA appendix are the big asks. Who owns the drafting?
[15:58] Tom Ellis: Redwood will own the first draft (Tom + Legal + Priya for tech appendix). We'll circulate and ask for marks.
[16:08] Devon Park: and we'll provide the telemetry samples right after this call.
[16:16] Priya Raman: on the technical mitigations — besides KV throttling, we also suggest a gentle GC window and a fast path for short-sequence requests to bypass KV when appropriate to reduce pressure.
[16:34] Marta Silva: bypassing KV worries us for correctness. how do you ensure deterministic outputs?
[16:44] Priya Raman: we can flag responses generated via fast-path and keep a small sample of full-kv outputs to validate regression. Also, maintain provenance headers.
[16:56] Tom Ellis: one other point: fallback routing can be limited by region; if the dedicated pool is only in us-west we may need regional fallbacks. We'll include regional routing statements.
[17:12] Devon Park: the incident showed fallback to eu was attempted and added latency. So region routing is important.
[17:24] Tom Ellis: noted — we'll make region-aware fallback policy explicit.
[17:30] [00:17:30] Jordan Lee: I'm adding notes to the shared doc now (link: https://redwood.example.com/archipelago/sla-appendix-v2).
[17:42] Marta Silva: one last ask from Security — can you provide a brief threat model for fallback modes showing attack surface when routing to quantized or dedicated pools?
[17:54] Lin Wu: yes please, that will go to our auditors.
[18:04] Priya Raman: we have a short threat model template; I'll adapt it for fallback modes and include the KMS/HSM callouts.
[18:16] Tom Ellis: great. Any other items?
[18:22] Elliot Chan: not from procurement. We'll wait for numbers and legal.
[18:28] Marta Silva: thanks everyone.
[18:32] Tom Ellis: recap of next steps — Tom sends SLA draft + appendix (due 6/12), Priya runs stress test and posts logs (due 6/11), Devon and Marta confirm latency SLO bands (due 6/09), Lin will request SOC2 appendix and review HSM details (due 6/10), Elliot to start procurement review (due 6/17).
[18:58] [00:18:58] Meeting ends.

Notes / Artifacts referenced:
- SLA appendix draft (link above)
- Stress test plan (Priya to upload to shared sheet)
- Cost tradeoff spreadsheet (Priya/Jordan)
- KMS/HSM integration diagram (Tom)

End of transcript.
